strengths: Comprehensive unified framework across three settings (finite models, bounded function classes, parametric models) with rigorous nonasymptotic regret analysis
Novel separation principle elegantly decoupling model identification and certainty-equivalent control, providing a fresh perspective distinct from optimism-based approaches
Nonasymptotic policy regret bounds with recovery of known linear system results as special cases, validating the theoretical framework
Practical algorithm simplicity for linear feature case requiring only Gaussian sampling with recursive least squares updates
Rigorous technical analysis with detailed proofs addressing state boundedness and benign transient behavior important to control applications
Multi-model perspective providing logarithmic (vs. polynomial) regret scaling in number of models compared to model-free alternatives
weaknesses: Strong restrictive assumptions limit applicability: (1) true model must be in class F (no model misspecification treatment), (2) Bellman-type inequality requires constructing cost-to-go function V and H₂ gain γ, (3) persistence of excitation (Assumption 3) involves system-dependent constants (ce) difficult to verify

Limited practical applicability: Algorithm 2 requires intractable ε-packing computation over infinite-dimensional spaces; Algorithm 3 requires solving dynamic programming at each iteration; tuning requires unknown problem-dependent constants (ce, Lᵥ, b, etc.)

Dimension-dependent regret blowup for general settings: packing number m(ε) scales as exp((L/ε)^(dₓ+dᵤ)) for Lipschitz functions, yielding O(N^((dₓ+dᵤ)/(dₓ+dᵤ+2))) scaling; effectively negates 'no-regret' claim in high dimensions

Severely weak experimental validation: only one 20-dimensional linear system example with no nonlinear systems tested, no comparisons with competing methods (optimism-based, two-step learning), no model misspecification experiments despite practical importance

Moderate technical novelty: core techniques (Lyapunov analysis, concentration inequalities, persistence of excitation) are standard from control theory and online learning; main novelty lies in combination rather than methodological innovation

Theory-practice gap: excitation schedule σ²ᵤₖ is theory-optimal but potentially suboptimal in practice; normalization factor 1 + |(x,u)|²/b² appears somewhat ad-hoc; no practical guidance for hyperparameter selection

strengths: Unified theoretical framework across three model classes (finite, bounded, parametric) with systematic analysis
Clean algorithmic principle separating model identification from control, applicable uniformly across settings
Recovery of known O(√Np) regret for linear dynamics validates the framework
Non-asymptotic finite-time regret bounds with explicit dependence on problem parameters
Comprehensive technical exposition with detailed proofs and treatment of special cases
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines well-established ideas (posterior sampling, certainty-equivalent control) without major conceptual innovation; S3 essentially recovers existing results from prior work

Restrictive assumptions: Bellman inequality requires knowing cost-to-go function V (assumes away the hard problem), smoothness conditions are strong, persistence of excitation depends on unknown problem-specific constants ce difficult to verify a priori

Regret bounds lack competitiveness: S1 is expected for model selection, S2 shows O(N^((dx+du)/(dx+du+2))) dimension-dependent scaling, S3 recovers known results without improvement; no lower bounds provided for optimality assessment

Questionable practical applicability despite claims: Algorithm 2 requires solving optimization+packing+DP per iteration (explicitly acknowledged as computationally intractable), requires pre-computed expensive DP solutions, depends on unknown hyperparameter constants, regret measured against unknown optimal policy—circular dependency unaddressed

Negligible experimental validation: only toy synthetic linear systems with dx=20,du=5, no comparison to baselines or prior methods, no real problems, no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; inadequate for demonstrating practical utility
Claims-evidence mismatch: paper claims simplicity and practical utility despite algorithms requiring solving hard subproblems and extensive hyperparameter tuning

Missing lower bounds and optimality assessment: no information-theoretic regret lower bounds; regret rates for S2 and S3 not demonstrated to be better than recent nonlinear control work (Kakade et al. 2020, Boffi et al. 2021)
Model mismatch not addressed: paper assumes f ∈ F but provides no analysis for model misspecification; deferred to future work despite being critical for practical applicability

strengths: Clear and interpretable regret bounds across three increasingly general settings with clean dependence on problem parameters (m for finite models, ε-packings for general classes, p for parametric models)
Elegant separation principle that decouples model identification from certainty-equivalent control, providing a fresh perspective relative to optimism-based approaches
Technically rigorous analysis with comprehensive proofs, skillful use of Lyapunov functions, and complete treatment in appendices
Simple and implementable algorithms, particularly Algorithm 1 which only requires sampling from softmax distributions
Principled framework that recovers linear systems as special case and connects to adaptive control literature
Addresses important practical considerations: boundedness of trajectories, finite-time convergence, persistence of excitation characterization for nonlinear systems
weaknesses: Strong and technical assumptions: Bellman-type inequality (Ass. 1) requires pre-specified value function; persistence of excitation (Ass. 3) with finite-b normalization is non-standard and hard to verify without knowing true model

Proof techniques are largely incremental: Lyapunov function analysis, concentration arguments, and packing-based discretization are well-established; novelty lies primarily in application rather than methodology
Model misspecification not addressed: all results assume f ∈ F. This fundamental limitation severely restricts practical applicability

Incomplete regret analysis: S2 bound has Nε² term leading to poor high-dimensional scaling O(N^{(d_x+d_u)/(d_x+d_u+2)}); S3 bound doesn't improve over linear systems despite additional parameters; no lower bounds provided
Insufficient experimental validation: only linear systems tested, no comparisons with baselines, no real applications, experiments primarily verify assumptions rather than demonstrate advantages

Computational complexity concerns: Algorithm 2 computationally intractable (continuous minimization, packing construction); Algorithm 3 requires DP at each step; paper sidesteps these by focusing on sample complexity only
Large hidden constants in regret bounds: c_α = e^{3c_2M} and other problem-dependent constants could be prohibitively large; practical magnitude not discussed
Benign transient claims only establish bounded second moments E[|x_k|²], not traditional stability for nonlinear systems; interpretation of almost-sure boundedness given unbounded noise is unclear

strengths: Novel frequentist regret analysis for posterior sampling RL in non-episodic nonlinear settings, combining tools from online learning, control theory, and statistics
Comprehensive theoretical framework covering three model classes (finite, bounded, parametric) with recovery of known linear system bounds
Rigorous technical treatment: Lyapunov-based decomposition, proper handling of coupled dynamics, persistence of excitation from system identification literature
Sound positioning relative to related work (optimism-based methods, multi-model adaptive control, prior posterior sampling RL)
Clear algorithmic descriptions with separation principle simplifying policy evaluation via MPC or PPO
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: algorithms are straightforward applications of Hedge and certainty equivalence; primary contribution is analysis rather than new techniques
Regret bounds contain hidden problem-dependent constants (c_α = e^(3c_2M), dependence on Δ, packing numbers m(ε)) that are not characterized; S1 bound becomes loose when models are similar

Restrictive assumptions: Bellman inequality (Ass. 1), persistence of excitation (Ass. 3) with ad-hoc normalization, realizability all exclude meaningful problem classes; constant tuning (η, σ²_uk depend on unknown Δ) limits practical applicability

Severely weak experimental validation: no comparison with baselines or alternative methods, only 2 experiments on toy problems, short horizons (~100-200 steps) insufficient to verify regret scaling, no empirical advantage demonstrated

Dense technical presentation obscures key insights; assumptions scattered across appendix; non-standard normalization term (1 + |(x_k,u_k)|²/b²) in Eq. (1) poorly motivated; Algorithm 2 (S2) acknowledged as computationally intractable

Gap between theory and practice: policy evaluation is acknowledged computational bottleneck (60ms/iter) but not addressed; discretization errors ignored; approximate policy evaluation not analyzed; step size requirements could be prohibitively restrictive

strengths: Technically sound analysis with rigorous proofs using Lyapunov functions, concentration arguments, and careful case decomposition for model selection
Comprehensive framework handling three problem settings (finite/infinite/parametric models) with appropriate complexity measures (packing numbers) for continuous systems
Addresses practical control concerns: stability guarantees (Eq. 3), finite-time convergence (Cor. C.6), boundedness of trajectories, and recovery of O(√(d_u Np)) rates for linear systems
Uses persistence of excitation assumptions from control theory, more suitable for continuous state-action systems than mixing conditions, handles dynamics near stability boundaries
Clear algorithmic separation principle enabling offline policy computation (MPC, DP) rather than expensive online optimization of confidence regions
weaknesses: Limited novelty: algorithmic framework closely follows Mania et al./Simchowitz-Foster; extension to nonlinear systems appears straightforward given existing machinery; posterior sampling + Hedge connection not fundamentally new

Restrictive and hard-to-verify assumptions: Bellman-type inequality (Ass. 1) excludes many nonlinear systems; persistence of excitation (Ass. 3) becomes loose when models are close (small Δ); realizability contradicts non-realizable pendulum experiment

Loose regret bounds with poor parameter dependence: S1 has O(1/Δ) dependence making bounds vacuous when models are nearby; S2 has explicit O(N) discretization error; bounds contain multiple unknown constants (c_r1, c_r2, c_r3) without magnitude guidance

Minimal experimental validation: only 2 experiments (linear + pendulum), no comparisons with optimism-based/Thompson sampling/baselines, contradicts realizability assumption without testing relaxations, limited scalability evidence

Significant theory-practice gap: algorithm requires unknown constants for tuning (Δ, L_V, L_l); persistence of excitation non-verifiable a priori; policy computation via MPC/DP equally expensive as confidence-set methods; claims of practical utility unsupported
Computational intractability of Setting S2: online packing (Algorithm 4) impractical for continuous function spaces; paper dismisses as 'learnability guarantees' rather than deployment-ready

Dense presentation obscuring insights: key algorithmic idea (posterior sampling + exploration) buried in technical details; motivation for normalization in Eq. (1) ad-hoc; critical results relegated to appendix; algorithm-to-proof connection unclear

Incomplete theoretical characterization: no lower bounds for nonlinear systems showing tightness; no robustness analysis when assumptions violated; coupling between Assumptions 1-3 unexplored; role of constant b poorly motivated

strengths: Addresses fundamental problem of online non-episodic RL with nonlinear dynamics, an important frontier in reinforcement learning theory
Novel unified framework bridging posterior sampling, Hedge updates, and control-theoretic tools (dissipativity); elegantly separates identification from control
Handles three distinct model settings (finite, infinite, parametric) with regret guarantees; avoids strong structural assumptions (contraction, linear parameterization)
Technically sophisticated proofs using Lyapunov analysis that handle dependent dynamics, correlated losses, and stability near boundaries
Validates approach by recovering O(√(d_u Np)) bounds for linear systems, matching prior work; persistence of excitation is weaker than mixing assumptions
Comprehensive treatment with finite-time convergence, bounded state guarantees, and extensive appendices; clear writing and well-organized presentation
Algorithms are simple, implementable, and naturally integrate with model predictive control; demonstrated ability to incorporate prior knowledge
Provides important connections between RL, online learning, and adaptive control communities
weaknesses: Restrictive assumptions: realizability (f ∈ F), persistence of excitation (Ass. 3 verification non-trivial for general nonlinear systems), smoothness requirements, and pre-existing Lyapunov function in Bellman inequality

Normalization parameter b in prediction error (Eq. 1) appears ad-hoc; while b→∞ case exists in appendix, treatment is cumbersome with complex constants; lacks practical guidance on parameter selection

Complex, unintuitive dependence on problem parameters: S1 regret depends on model separation Δ (problematic when indistinguishable), S2 requires joint optimization over discretization ε and has unclear packing number dependence
Limited experimental validation: only two examples, no algorithmic baselines, no ablation studies on model quality/dimension dependence; pendulum example violates realizability assumption

Significant computational concerns inadequately addressed: S2 requires intractable online ε-packing; S3 requires expensive policy evaluation via DP/MPC at each iteration; claims of practicality unsupported by complexity analysis
Constants in regret bounds not tightly controlled (e.g., c_α = e^{3c_2M}); practical regret could be large, empirically unvalidated against alternatives
Modest novelty for linear systems (directly recovers prior work); generalization to nonlinear is non-trivial but incremental in this aspect
Incomplete analysis of central Assumption 3: verification for general nonlinear systems limited to specific structures (controllability conditions); generic applicability unclear
